investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: Why can the dipstick blood pad be positive with no red cells on microscopy?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back: It detects haem peroxidase activity, so free myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis) and free haemoglobin (intravascular haemolysis) also turn it positive. Confirm true haematuria with microscopy.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: What important urinary protein does the dipstick MISS, and what does this mean clinically?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back: It detects albumin but not Bence-Jones protein (free light chains). Myeloma can therefore give dipstick-negative proteinuria; send urine/serum electrophoresis or free light chains if suspected.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: Why can nitrites be falsely negative in a genuine UTI?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back: Nitrite needs nitrate-reducing bacteria (e.g. E. coli) and several hours of bladder dwell time. Frequent voiding, dilute urine, low dietary nitrate, or non-reducers (Enterococcus, Staph. saprophyticus) give false negatives.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: At roughly what blood glucose does glycosuria appear on dipstick, and what are non-diabetic causes?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back: Glycosuria appears once serum glucose exceeds the renal threshold of about 10 mmol/L. Non-diabetic causes include pregnancy, renal glycosuria (low threshold) and SGLT2 inhibitor therapy.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: How do you interpret bilirubin and urobilinogen together on a dipstick?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back:
• Bilirubin +ve with RAISED urobilinogen → hepatocellular jaundice (e.g. hepatitis).
  • Bilirubin +ve with LOW/absent urobilinogen → obstructive (post-hepatic) jaundice — conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and spills into urine, but none reaches the gut.
  • Raised urobilinogen with bilirubin NEGATIVE → pre-hepatic/haemolysis.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: What is the classic threshold for significant bacteriuria on urine culture (Kass criterion)?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back: ≥10⁵ CFU/mL of a single organism. In a symptomatic patient with pyuria, lower counts (10³–10⁴ CFU/mL) are also considered clinically significant.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: How should a standard urine sample for MC&S be collected, and why?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back:
Midstream clean-catch (MSU):
  • clean the meatus
  • void the first stream into the toilet
  • then collect the middle stream.
Discarding the first portion flushes away distal urethral/perineal flora and reduces contamination.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: What does mixed growth (≥3 organisms) or squamous epithelial cells on urine microscopy suggest?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back: Contamination of the sample with perineal/skin flora rather than true infection. The specimen should be repeated with a properly collected MSU.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: Give the differential for sterile pyuria (WBCs present, routine culture negative).
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back:
• Renal TB
  • Chlamydia/gonococcal urethritis
  • recently or partially treated UTI
  • renal stones
  • indwelling catheter
  • interstitial cystitis
  • and urinary tract tumours.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: When should asymptomatic bacteriuria be treated with antibiotics?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back: Only in pregnancy (risk of pyelonephritis and preterm birth) or before urological instrumentation/surgery. Otherwise it should not be treated, to avoid promoting resistance.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: What protein forms the matrix of all urinary casts?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back: Tamm-Horsfall protein (uromodulin), secreted by the thick ascending limb and distal tubule.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: A red cell (RBC) cast in the urine indicates what?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back: Glomerulonephritis / nephritic syndrome — it is pathognomonic of glomerular bleeding and warrants urgent GN workup.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: Which cast is characteristic of acute tubular necrosis?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back: Granular 'muddy brown' casts (made of degenerated tubular epithelial cell debris).

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: What do white cell casts signify?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back: Pyelonephritis or acute interstitial nephritis (infection/inflammation of the tubulointerstitium).

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: What is the significance of waxy/broad casts versus hyaline casts?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back:
• Waxy/broad casts indicate chronic/advanced kidney disease (dilated atrophic tubules)
  • hyaline casts are benign and normal (dehydration, exercise, diuretics).

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: What is the main strength and main weakness of urine cytology in urothelial carcinoma?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back:
• Strength: high specificity, especially for high-grade tumours and carcinoma in situ (CIS)
  • Weakness: low sensitivity, particularly for low-grade papillary tumours which shed bland, cohesive cells.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: Why is a first morning (overnight) urine sample avoided for cytology?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back: Cells degenerate during prolonged overnight bladder residence, producing poor preservation and a high false-negative rate. A fresh mid-morning voided sample is preferred.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: How does a bladder-wash (barbotage) specimen compare with a voided specimen?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back: Bladder washings collected at cystoscopy yield more numerous, better-preserved cells and give higher sensitivity than a voided urine sample.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: Does a negative urine cytology exclude bladder cancer in a patient with visible haematuria?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back: No. Cystoscopy is mandatory in visible haematuria regardless of cytology, because cytology misses low-grade tumours. It is an adjunct, not a replacement for cystoscopy.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: Which bladder lesion is urine cytology especially valuable for detecting, and why?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back: Carcinoma in situ (CIS): it is a flat, high-grade lesion that is often invisible at cystoscopy but sheds highly atypical cells that cytology detects readily.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: What are the NICE 2-week-wait referral triggers for suspected urological cancer with haematuria?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back: Visible (macroscopic) haematuria in anyone ≥45 that is unexplained (or persists/recurs after treating a UTI), and unexplained non-visible haematuria in anyone ≥60 with dysuria or a raised white-cell count. Refer on a 2-week-wait pathway; flexible cystoscopy plus upper-tract imaging is the workup.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: How does urine microscopy distinguish glomerular from urological (lower-tract) haematuria?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back:
• Glomerular: dysmorphic red cells, red-cell casts, and significant proteinuria → refer nephrology for a glomerulonephritis workup.
  • Urological: isolated monomorphic red cells with no casts or protein → imaging and cystoscopy for a stone or tumour.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.front: Which urinary cast indicates nephrotic syndrome, and how is it identified?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.back: Fatty casts / oval fat bodies, showing a “Maltese cross” appearance under polarised light — a marker of heavy (nephrotic-range) proteinuria and lipiduria. (Contrast the nephritic marker: red-cell casts of glomerulonephritis.)

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: What does the urine protein:creatinine ratio (PCR) correct for, and why?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: It corrects for urine concentration by dividing protein by creatinine. Creatinine is excreted at a fairly constant rate, so a spot sample approximates 24-hour protein excretion without a timed collection.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: What are the units of PCR and the normal value?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: Units are mg/mmol. Normal PCR is <15 mg/mmol.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: What PCR value defines nephrotic-range proteinuria and what 24h excretion does it equate to?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: PCR >300–350 mg/mmol, equating to >3–3.5 g of protein per 24 hours.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: Why is ACR preferred over PCR for early diabetic and CKD screening?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: PCR measures total protein and is less sensitive at low levels. ACR specifically detects small amounts of albumin, so it picks up the early albuminuria of diabetic nephropathy and CKD that PCR may miss.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: Give the quick conversion between PCR and daily protein loss.
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: PCR in mg/mmol divided by ~100 approximates grams of protein per 24 hours (e.g. PCR 100 ≈ 1 g/day, PCR 300 ≈ 3 g/day).

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: What is the preferred first-line test to screen for early diabetic nephropathy, and what units does it use?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: Urine albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR), reported in mg/mmol on a first early-morning sample. It is more sensitive/specific for albumin than dipstick or PCR.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: State the three KDIGO albuminuria bands by ACR value.
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back:
• A1 <3 mg/mmol (normal/mildly increased)
  • A2 3–30 mg/mmol (moderately increased / 'microalbuminuria')
  • A3 >30 mg/mmol (severely increased / 'macroalbuminuria').

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: Why is an early-morning (first-pass) urine sample preferred for ACR?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: Overnight recumbency minimises orthostatic and exercise-induced albuminuria, giving the most reproducible result and reducing false positives.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: In diabetes, what does a confirmed ACR ≥3 mg/mmol prompt you to start, even with normal blood pressure?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: An ACE inhibitor or ARB, to slow progression of diabetic nephropathy. The raised ACR should be confirmed as persistent first.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: ACR vs PCR: when do you use each?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back:
• ACR for early detection of low-level albuminuria (diabetes/CKD screening)
  • PCR for quantifying heavy, established proteinuria.
ACR may miss non-albumin proteins like Bence Jones light chains.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: What does a urine osmolality greater than serum osmolality indicate?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: The kidney is actively concentrating urine, meaning ADH (vasopressin) is present and acting. Urine osm can normally reach ~1200 mOsm/kg with maximal ADH.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: In hyponatraemia, what does a urine osmolality <100 mOsm/kg signify?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: Appropriate ADH suppression with dilute urine. Causes are primary polydipsia and beer potomania / low-solute intake, where water intake overwhelms excretion but the kidney responds correctly.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: What are the three core criteria for diagnosing SIADH?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back:
• Clinical euvolaemia
  • inappropriately high urine osmolality (>100, usually >300 mOsm/kg) despite low serum osm
  • and high urine sodium (>30 mmol/L).
Thyroid and adrenal dysfunction must be excluded first.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: How does the water deprivation + DDAVP test distinguish cranial from nephrogenic DI?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: After deprivation urine osm stays low in both. Giving desmopressin raises urine osm by ≥50% in cranial (central) DI but produces no response in nephrogenic DI, where the kidney cannot respond to ADH.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: What urine osmolality after water deprivation effectively excludes diabetes insipidus?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: A urine osmolality rising above ~600 mOsm/kg, indicating intact concentrating ability. This pattern fits primary polydipsia rather than cranial or nephrogenic DI.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: Spot urine sodium <20 mmol/L in AKI — interpretation?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: A sodium-avid kidney: prerenal AKI from true hypovolaemia or reduced effective circulating volume (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome). The tubule is intact and reabsorbing sodium appropriately.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: Urine sodium >40 mmol/L in a patient with AKI suggests what?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) — damaged tubular cells cannot reabsorb sodium, so it leaks into the urine. Also seen with salt-wasting and, in euvolaemic hyponatraemia, SIADH.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: In metabolic alkalosis, why use urine chloride rather than urine sodium?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: Bicarbonaturia obligates sodium loss even when the patient is volume-depleted, so urine sodium can be falsely high. Urine chloride reflects true volume status: <20 = chloride-responsive (saline-responsive), >20 = chloride-resistant.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: Chloride-responsive vs chloride-resistant metabolic alkalosis — causes and treatment?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back:
• Chloride-responsive (U_Cl <20): vomiting, NG suction, diuretics, volume depletion — corrects with IV saline.
  • Chloride-resistant (U_Cl >20): hyperaldosteronism, Cushing, Bartter/Gitelman — does not correct with saline.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: Hypokalaemia with urine potassium <20 vs >20 mmol/L?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back:
• <20 = appropriate renal conservation, so loss is GI (diarrhoea/laxatives) or poor intake.
  • >20 = inappropriate renal potassium wasting: diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, renal tubular acidosis, or magnesium depletion.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: What is the formula for the fractional excretion of sodium (FENa)?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: FENa (%) = (urine Na × plasma Cr) ÷ (plasma Na × urine Cr) × 100. It corrects urine sodium for urinary concentration, making it more reliable than spot urine sodium alone.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: What FENa values distinguish pre-renal AKI from ATN?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back:
• FENa < 1% indicates pre-renal AKI (sodium-avid, intact tubules)
  • FENa > 2% indicates intrinsic AKI / ATN (injured tubules cannot reabsorb sodium).
Values of 1–2% are indeterminate.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: Why does FENa fail in a patient on diuretics, and what is used instead?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: Loop/thiazide diuretics force natriuresis, falsely raising FENa in a pre-renal patient. Use fractional excretion of urea (FEUrea) instead — FEUrea < 35% favours pre-renal because urea handling is diuretic-independent.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: What are the supporting urinary findings in pre-renal AKI versus ATN?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back:
• Pre-renal: urine Na < 20 mmol/L, urine osm > 500 mOsm/kg (concentrated), bland/hyaline casts.
  • ATN: urine Na > 40 mmol/L, urine osm < 350 (isosthenuric), muddy-brown granular casts.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: Name settings where FENa is unreliable or misleadingly low despite intrinsic injury.
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back:
FENa can be < 1% in
  • contrast nephropathy
  • rhabdomyolysis
  • early sepsis
  • hepatorenal syndrome
  • and acute glomerulonephritis.
It is also elevated at baseline in CKD due to adaptive natriuresis.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: Beyond an ACE inhibitor/ARB, what drug class is now added for albuminuric CKD?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back: An SGLT2 inhibitor (e.g. dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) provides additional renoprotection in diabetic AND non-diabetic CKD with albuminuria (DAPA-CKD/EMPA-KIDNEY; NICE). Combined with an ACE-i/ARB it slows GFR decline and reduces progression — a high-yield modern finals point.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.front: What is the management of SIADH versus cranial and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.back:
• SIADH: treat the cause + fluid restriction (hypertonic saline if acutely symptomatic; correct Na slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination).
  • Cranial DI: desmopressin.
  • Nephrogenic DI: treat the cause, low-salt/low-protein diet and a thiazide (paradoxically reduces urine output).

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: What is Bence-Jones protein?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back: Monoclonal free immunoglobulin light chains (kappa or lambda) present in the urine, classically due to multiple myeloma or AL amyloidosis.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: Why can a standard urine dipstick be negative in Bence-Jones proteinuria?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back: The dipstick protein pad detects ALBUMIN only. Free light chains are not albumin, so the dipstick can be negative despite heavy light-chain proteinuria. Urine protein electrophoresis/immunofixation is needed.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: Which tests make up the modern myeloma screen for detecting light chains?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back:
• Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP)
  • serum free light chain (sFLC) assay with kappa/lambda ratio
  • and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: How do urinary light chains cause acute kidney injury?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back: Filtered light chains precipitate with Tamm-Horsfall protein to form obstructive tubular casts (cast nephropathy / 'myeloma kidney'), plus direct proximal tubular toxicity, causing AKI.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: What is the normal serum free light chain kappa/lambda ratio, and what does an abnormal ratio suggest?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back: Normal ratio is approximately 0.26–1.65. A ratio outside this range indicates a clonal excess of one light chain type, supporting a plasma cell dyscrasia.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: Which specific molecule does a urine pregnancy test detect, and what produces it?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back: The beta-subunit of human chorionic gonadotrophin (beta-hCG), secreted by placental syncytiotrophoblast. Antibodies target the beta-subunit to avoid cross-reaction with LH, FSH and TSH.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: What is the typical sensitivity threshold of a modern urine hCG device, and when does it first become positive?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back: About 25 IU/L. Urinary hCG is usually detectable roughly 1–2 weeks post-conception, around the time of the missed period; first morning urine gives the earliest reliable positive.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: List the main causes of a false-negative urine pregnancy test.
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back:
• Testing too early (hCG below threshold)
  • dilute urine
  • and the hook effect where very high hCG (molar or multiple pregnancy) saturates the antibodies.
Diluting the sample and retesting overcomes the hook effect.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: In a normal early intrauterine pregnancy, how should serum beta-hCG change over 48 hours?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back: It should rise by at least 63%. A rise below this, a plateau, or a fall suggests an ectopic or non-viable pregnancy.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: A positive urine hCG with abdominal pain and PV bleeding should be treated as what until proven otherwise?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back: An ectopic pregnancy. A urine test confirms pregnancy but never its location, so urgent assessment (USS and serum beta-hCG) is required.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: How is the urine anion gap calculated and what does it estimate?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back: Urine anion gap = (urine Na+ + urine K+) − urine Cl−. It is an indirect surrogate for urinary ammonium (NH4+) excretion, used to work up a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: In NAGMA, what does a NEGATIVE vs POSITIVE urine anion gap indicate?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back:
• Negative UAG = high NH4+ excretion = extrarenal cause (GI bicarbonate loss, e.g. diarrhoea).
  • Positive UAG = impaired NH4+ excretion = renal tubular acidosis.
'Neg = GI, pos = kidney.'

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: What are the defining features of Type 1 (distal) RTA?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back:
• Failure to secrete H+ distally so the urine cannot be acidified below pH 5.5
  • hypokalaemia
  • and complications of nephrocalcinosis and renal stones.
It gives a positive urine anion gap.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: How does potassium help distinguish the RTA types?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back:
• Types 1 (distal) and 2 (proximal) are HYPOkalaemic.
  • Type 4 is HYPERkalaemic (hypoaldosteronism/aldosterone resistance, e.g. diabetes, ACE inhibitors).

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: When is the urine anion gap unreliable?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back: When ammonium is excreted with an unmeasured anion other than chloride (ketoacidosis, toluene/glue-sniffing hippurate, D-lactic acidosis) making it falsely positive, and in oliguria with urine Na+ < 20 mmol/L.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: Which stone type is commonest and how does it appear on plain X-ray?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back: Calcium oxalate (~80% of stones) and it is radio-opaque (visible on plain KUB).

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: Which urinary stone is radiolucent, and what urine pH and condition favour it?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back: Uric acid stones are radiolucent (missed on plain film). They form in persistently acidic urine (pH < 5.5) and are associated with gout / high purine turnover.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: What does a LOW urinary citrate on 24h screen signify, and what is the treatment?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back: Citrate is a natural inhibitor of calcium crystallisation; low citrate (hypocitraturia) is a risk factor for stones. Treat with potassium citrate, which also raises urinary pH. Classically low in distal renal tubular acidosis.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: A staghorn calculus in alkaline urine with a Proteus UTI is made of what, and why must it be completely removed?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back: Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate), an infection stone from urease-producing organisms. Any residual fragment is a nidus for persistent infection, regrowth and recurrent urosepsis, so complete clearance is essential.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: First-line dietary advice given to essentially ALL stone formers, and one counter-intuitive point about calcium.
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back: Increase fluids to keep urine output > 2.5 L/day, moderate sodium and animal protein. Do NOT restrict dietary calcium — low calcium intake increases oxalate absorption and worsens stone risk.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.front: How is each type of renal tubular acidosis treated?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.back:
• Type 1 (distal) and Type 2 (proximal) → oral alkali (sodium bicarbonate or potassium citrate); type 2 needs high doses plus potassium supplements (± a thiazide to reduce dosing).
  • Type 4 (hyperkalaemic) → low-potassium diet + fludrocortisone (or a loop diuretic) and review/stop offending drugs (ACE-i/ARB, NSAIDs, potassium-sparing diuretics).

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.question: A 68-year-old man with back pain, anaemia and acute kidney injury has a urine dipstick that is negative for protein. Which statement is correct?
options: Bence-Jones protein is detected strongly by the protein pad
The dipstick may miss Bence-Jones protein, so send urine electrophoresis if myeloma is suspected
Proteinuria in myeloma is always albumin-based
The negative result confirms the kidneys are normal
A negative protein pad reliably excludes significant proteinuria
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.answer: The dipstick may miss Bence-Jones protein, so send urine electrophoresis if myeloma is suspected
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.explanation: The protein pad detects albumin but is insensitive to free light chains (Bence-Jones protein). In suspected myeloma the correct step is urine and serum protein electrophoresis or free light chain assay regardless of a negative dipstick.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.question: A woman with dysuria and frequency has a dipstick positive for leucocyte esterase but negative for nitrites. What is the best interpretation?
options: She must have a fungal infection
Leucocyte esterase always indicates renal stones
The result is uninterpretable and should be discarded
UTI is excluded because nitrites are negative
UTI remains likely; a negative nitrite does not exclude it
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.answer: UTI remains likely; a negative nitrite does not exclude it
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.explanation: Nitrite requires nitrate-reducing bacteria and adequate bladder dwell time, so false negatives are common with frequent voiding or non-reducing organisms. In a symptomatic woman with pyuria, UTI is still likely and should be treated with an MSU sent for culture.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.question: A patient is found to have a strongly blood-positive dipstick, but microscopy shows no red blood cells. Which cause best explains this?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.explanation: The blood pad reacts to haem peroxidase activity, so free myoglobin turns it positive without any red cells present. Rhabdomyolysis releases myoglobin, producing a blood-positive dipstick with negative microscopy.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.question: A 25-year-old non-pregnant woman has dysuria and frequency. Her MSU culture grows Escherichia coli at 10⁴ CFU/mL with pyuria on microscopy. How should this result be interpreted?
options: Contamination, as the count is below 10⁵ CFU/mL
Normal urine with no evidence of infection
Asymptomatic bacteriuria that should be left untreated
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.explanation: In a symptomatic patient with pyuria, a single-organism count of 10³–10⁴ CFU/mL is accepted as clinically significant. The combination of typical symptoms, pyuria, and a pure uropathogen supports treating this as a genuine UTI.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.question: A 40-year-old man has persistent frequency and microscopy shows pyuria, but routine urine culture is repeatedly negative. Which investigation is most important to exclude a serious cause?
options: Repeat midstream urine for routine culture
Three early-morning urine samples for mycobacterial culture
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.answer: Three early-morning urine samples for mycobacterial culture
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.explanation: Persistent sterile pyuria is a classic pointer to renal tuberculosis, which does not grow on standard media. Three early-morning urine samples for acid-fast bacilli and mycobacterial culture are the key test to exclude it.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.question: Screening MSU in a 28-year-old pregnant woman grows Escherichia coli at 10⁵ CFU/mL, but she has no urinary symptoms. What is the correct management?
options: No treatment, as she is asymptomatic
Treat with an appropriate antibiotic guided by sensitivities
Treat only if she later develops symptoms
Reassure and repeat culture in the third trimester only
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.answer: Treat with an appropriate antibiotic guided by sensitivities
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is one of the few situations that mandates antibiotic treatment, because untreated infection risks ascending pyelonephritis and preterm birth. Therapy should be guided by the culture sensitivities and a pregnancy-safe agent chosen.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.question: A 30-year-old man presents with haematuria, hypertension and oedema two weeks after a sore throat. Urine microscopy shows red cell casts. Which diagnosis do these casts point to?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.explanation: Red cell casts form when erythrocytes cross a damaged glomerular basement membrane and are moulded within the tubule. They are pathognomonic of glomerular bleeding and, with the post-streptococcal history and nephritic features, indicate glomerulonephritis.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.question: A patient develops oliguric acute kidney injury after prolonged hypotension in theatre. Urine microscopy shows 'muddy brown' granular casts. What is the most likely cause?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.explanation: Ischaemic injury sloughs tubular epithelial cells that degenerate into pigmented granular debris, forming muddy-brown casts. This finding after a hypotensive insult is the classic sediment of acute tubular necrosis.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.question: Which urinary cast is a benign finding that can appear in healthy individuals after strenuous exercise or dehydration?
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.explanation: Hyaline casts consist almost entirely of Tamm-Horsfall protein with no cellular inclusions, forming when urine is concentrated and low in flow. They are non-specific and seen in health with dehydration, exercise or loop diuretic use.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.question: A 68-year-old smoker with visible haematuria has a negative urine cytology result. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat urine cytology in 6 months and take no further action now
Start empirical antibiotics for presumed infection
Reassure the patient that bladder cancer is excluded
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.explanation: Visible haematuria mandates cystoscopy irrespective of the cytology result. Urine cytology has low sensitivity for low-grade tumours, so a negative result cannot exclude malignancy and cystoscopy remains the essential investigation.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.question: For which type of urothelial lesion is urine cytology most sensitive?
options: High-grade carcinoma including carcinoma in situ
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.answer: High-grade carcinoma including carcinoma in situ
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.explanation: High-grade tumours and CIS shed discohesive cells with marked nuclear atypia that cytology detects reliably. Cytology is particularly valuable for CIS, which is a flat lesion often missed on cystoscopy.

investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.question: Which specimen and handling approach gives the highest-yield urine cytology result?
options: Urine from a long-term indwelling catheter bag
First-void overnight urine sent the following day
A dilute sample taken immediately after high fluid intake
A bladder-wash (barbotage) specimen collected at cystoscopy
A single voided sample after 48 hours at room temperature
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.answer: A bladder-wash (barbotage) specimen collected at cystoscopy
investigations__URINE__Dipstick & Micros.explanation: Bladder washings provide abundant, well-preserved cells and higher sensitivity than voided urine. Overnight, delayed, catheter, and dilute samples all suffer from cellular degeneration or reactive atypia that degrade accuracy.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.question: What are the standard reporting units for a urine protein:creatinine ratio (PCR)?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.explanation: PCR is reported as milligrams of protein per millimole of creatinine (mg/mmol). This ratio corrects urinary protein for urine concentration using creatinine.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.question: A PCR of >300–350 mg/mmol corresponds to which of the following?
options: Isolated tubular proteinuria within normal limits
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.explanation: A PCR above 300–350 mg/mmol equates to more than 3–3.5 g of protein per 24 hours, which defines nephrotic-range proteinuria. This warrants urgent nephrology assessment, especially with oedema and hypoalbuminaemia.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.question: Which test is preferred over PCR for early screening of diabetic nephropathy and CKD?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.explanation: ACR specifically measures albumin and is more sensitive at low levels of urinary protein loss. NICE recommends ACR as the first-line test to detect the early albuminuria of diabetes and CKD, which PCR can miss.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.question: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes attends his annual review. His early-morning urine ACR is 18 mg/mmol, confirmed on a repeat sample. Which KDIGO albuminuria category does this represent?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.explanation: An ACR of 3–30 mg/mmol defines the A2 band, moderately increased albuminuria (formerly microalbuminuria). This is the earliest detectable sign of diabetic nephropathy and warrants intervention.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.question: A patient with type 1 diabetes has a persistent ACR of 8 mg/mmol with a normal blood pressure of 118/74 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start an ACE inhibitor or ARB
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.answer: Start an ACE inhibitor or ARB
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.explanation: A confirmed ACR ≥3 mg/mmol in diabetes is an indication to start an ACE inhibitor or ARB even when blood pressure is normal, to slow nephropathy progression. These agents reduce intraglomerular pressure and albuminuria.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.question: Which statement best describes the correct use of ACR compared with protein:creatinine ratio (PCR)?
options: PCR must be measured on a 24-hour timed collection only
ACR is best for quantifying heavy established proteinuria
ACR is more sensitive for early low-level albuminuria and is preferred for screening
ACR reliably detects Bence Jones light-chain proteinuria
PCR is the recommended screen for early diabetic nephropathy
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.answer: ACR is more sensitive for early low-level albuminuria and is preferred for screening
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.explanation: ACR detects the small amounts of albumin that mark early glomerular disease, making it the preferred screening test in diabetes and CKD. PCR is reserved for quantifying heavier, established proteinuria.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.question: A 68-year-old on no diuretics has serum Na 122 mmol/L, serum osm 258 mOsm/kg, urine osm 480 mOsm/kg and urine Na 55 mmol/L. He is clinically euvolaemic with normal thyroid and cortisol. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.explanation: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine (osm >100) and high urine Na (>30) after excluding thyroid and adrenal disease defines SIADH. ADH is being secreted despite low serum osmolality, so the kidney concentrates urine when it should be diluting it.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.question: A patient with polyuria undergoes a water deprivation test. Urine osmolality remains low at 180 mOsm/kg after deprivation, then rises to 620 mOsm/kg after desmopressin. Which condition does this indicate?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.explanation: Failure to concentrate on deprivation with a robust rise in urine osmolality after exogenous desmopressin identifies cranial DI, where endogenous ADH is deficient but the kidney responds normally to replacement. A nephrogenic kidney would not respond to DDAVP.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.question: A young man drinking large volumes of water presents with serum Na 128 mmol/L. Which urine osmolality result best fits primary polydipsia as the cause?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.explanation: In primary polydipsia ADH is appropriately suppressed, so the kidney produces maximally dilute urine below 100 mOsm/kg. This distinguishes it from SIADH, where urine remains inappropriately concentrated.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.question: A 78-year-old with vomiting and reduced urine output has an AKI. A spot urine sodium is 12 mmol/L. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.explanation: A urine sodium below 20 mmol/L indicates the tubule is reabsorbing sodium avidly in response to reduced effective circulating volume. In a hypovolaemic patient with vomiting this is classic prerenal AKI. ATN would instead show a urine sodium above 40 mmol/L.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.question: A patient with recurrent vomiting has a metabolic alkalosis. Urine sodium is 45 mmol/L but urine chloride is 10 mmol/L. What does this indicate?
options: Chloride-responsive alkalosis that will correct with IV saline
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.answer: Chloride-responsive alkalosis that will correct with IV saline
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.explanation: In metabolic alkalosis bicarbonaturia drags sodium out, so urine sodium is misleadingly high; urine chloride is the true marker. A urine chloride below 20 mmol/L defines a chloride-responsive alkalosis, consistent with vomiting and volume depletion, which corrects with saline.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.question: A hypokalaemic patient has a spot urine potassium of 45 mmol/L. Which is the best conclusion?
options: The kidney is conserving potassium appropriately
There is inappropriate renal potassium wasting
The result confirms transcellular shift only
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.answer: There is inappropriate renal potassium wasting
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.explanation: In hypokalaemia the kidney should conserve potassium and produce a urine potassium below 20 mmol/L. A value above 20 mmol/L indicates inappropriate renal wasting, pointing to diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, renal tubular acidosis, or magnesium depletion.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.question: A 70-year-old man with vomiting and hypotension has an AKI. Spot indices: urine Na 12 mmol/L, urine osmolality 620 mOsm/kg, FENa 0.4%. Which is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate first step?
options: Pre-renal AKI — give a fluid challenge
Acute interstitial nephritis — stop the offending drug
Acute tubular necrosis — supportive management only
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.answer: Pre-renal AKI — give a fluid challenge
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.explanation: A FENa < 1% with low urine sodium and concentrated urine (> 500 mOsm/kg) reflects sodium-avid tubules responding to hypoperfusion. The clinical picture of volume loss supports a fluid challenge as first-line management.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.question: A patient with AKI on regular furosemide has a FENa of 3%. How should this result be interpreted?
options: It indicates the patient is euvolaemic and needs no assessment
It confirms ATN and diuretics can be ignored
FENa is unreliable here; calculate FEUrea instead
It confirms pre-renal AKI because the value is elevated
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.answer: FENa is unreliable here; calculate FEUrea instead
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.explanation: Loop diuretics cause natriuresis that artefactually raises FENa, so a value of 3% cannot be trusted to indicate ATN in this patient. FEUrea is diuretic-independent, and a value below 35% would favour a pre-renal state.

investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.question: Which urinary sediment finding most specifically supports a diagnosis of acute tubular necrosis?
investigations__URINE__Renal Function &.explanation: Muddy-brown granular casts arise from sloughed, degenerated tubular epithelial cells and are the classic sediment finding of ATN. Hyaline or bland sediment points to pre-renal disease, while red cell casts indicate glomerulonephritis.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.question: A 68-year-old man with back pain, anaemia and raised creatinine has a urine dipstick that is negative for protein. Myeloma is suspected. Which investigation best detects urinary Bence-Jones protein?
options: Urine microscopy for red cell casts
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.explanation: The dipstick detects only albumin, so it misses free light chains. Urine protein electrophoresis identifies a monoclonal band and immunofixation confirms and types it as kappa or lambda.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.question: Why is a standard urine dipstick unreliable for excluding Bence-Jones proteinuria?
options: It is affected by urine pH above 7
It requires a 24-hour sample to work
It only detects albumin, not free light chains
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.answer: It only detects albumin, not free light chains
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.explanation: The dipstick protein pad is designed to bind albumin. Monoclonal free light chains are chemically different, so they are not detected and the dipstick can read negative despite significant light-chain proteinuria.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.question: A patient with known multiple myeloma develops rapidly rising creatinine. Heavy urinary free light chain excretion is most directly responsible for which renal complication?
options: Cast nephropathy causing acute kidney injury
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.answer: Cast nephropathy causing acute kidney injury
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.explanation: Filtered light chains are nephrotoxic and precipitate with Tamm-Horsfall protein to form obstructing tubular casts. This cast nephropathy, or myeloma kidney, is a classic cause of AKI in myeloma.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.question: A 24-year-old woman has a strongly positive urine pregnancy test but a recent ultrasound showed a molar pregnancy with very high hCG levels. On a repeat clinic device her urine test unexpectedly reads negative. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The hook (prozone) effect from extremely high hCG saturating the antibodies
The device detects only the alpha-subunit of hCG
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.answer: The hook (prozone) effect from extremely high hCG saturating the antibodies
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.explanation: In molar and multiple pregnancies hCG can be so high that it saturates both capture and detection antibodies, preventing the sandwich complex from forming and giving a false-negative result. Diluting the urine and retesting restores a correct positive.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.question: Before which of the following is a urine hCG test most clearly mandatory in a woman of childbearing age?
options: A CT abdomen and starting methotrexate
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.answer: A CT abdomen and starting methotrexate
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.explanation: Ionising radiation and teratogenic drugs such as methotrexate can seriously harm a fetus, so pregnancy must be excluded first. Non-invasive, non-teratogenic tests carry no such requirement.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.question: A woman with a positive urine pregnancy test attends with left iliac fossa pain and light vaginal bleeding. Her serum beta-hCG has risen only 20% over 48 hours. What does this pattern most strongly suggest?
options: A completed miscarriage with no remaining hCG
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.explanation: A normal early intrauterine pregnancy raises serum beta-hCG by at least 63% over 48 hours, so a rise of only 20% is abnormal. Combined with pain and bleeding this pattern strongly points to an ectopic pregnancy requiring urgent assessment.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.question: A patient has a hyperchloraemic (normal anion gap) metabolic acidosis. The urine anion gap is calculated as +32. Which mechanism does this most strongly support?
options: Loss of hydrochloric acid through vomiting
Impaired renal ammonium excretion (renal tubular acidosis)
Accumulation of unmeasured plasma anions such as lactate
Respiratory compensation for a metabolic alkalosis
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.answer: Impaired renal ammonium excretion (renal tubular acidosis)
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.explanation: A positive urine anion gap indicates low urinary NH4+ excretion, meaning the kidney is failing to excrete acid appropriately. In the context of a normal anion gap acidosis this points to renal tubular acidosis rather than a gastrointestinal cause.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.question: A woman with recurrent renal calculi is found to have a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, hypokalaemia, and a urine pH of 6.2 that will not fall below 5.5 despite the systemic acidosis. Which diagnosis fits best?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.explanation: Inability to acidify the urine below pH 5.5 despite systemic acidosis is the hallmark of distal (Type 1) RTA due to failed distal H+ secretion. It is classically associated with hypokalaemia and nephrocalcinosis or stones.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.question: A patient with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease taking an ACE inhibitor has a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with hyperkalaemia and a urine pH of 5.1. Which type of renal tubular acidosis is this?
options: No RTA — this is a high anion gap acidosis
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.explanation: Type 4 RTA is the hyperkalaemic form, caused by hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone resistance, commonly seen in diabetes and with ACE inhibitors. Reduced ammonium production limits acid excretion, but the distal nephron can still acidify the urine below pH 5.5.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.question: A 34-year-old man with recurrent renal colic has a plain KUB X-ray reported as normal, but CT KUB shows a 7 mm calculus. His 24h urine pH is consistently 5.2. What is the most likely stone composition?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.explanation: Uric acid stones are radiolucent and therefore invisible on plain KUB while clearly seen on CT. They form in persistently acidic urine (pH < 5.5), matching this patient's pH of 5.2. Management includes urinary alkalinisation to pH 6.5–7 and allopurinol.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.question: A woman with a chronic Proteus mirabilis urinary tract infection is found to have a large staghorn calculus and a urine pH of 7.8. What is the most appropriate priority in management?
options: Long-term suppressive antibiotics alone with observation
Complete surgical removal of the stone
Thiazide diuretic to reduce urinary calcium
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.answer: Complete surgical removal of the stone
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.explanation: This is a struvite infection stone driven by urease-producing Proteus in alkaline urine. Any residual fragment harbours bacteria and acts as a nidus for regrowth and recurrent urosepsis, so complete removal is essential. Antibiotics are adjunctive but cannot sterilise a retained stone.

investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.question: On a 24h urine metabolic screen, which single finding is a protective factor whose LOW value increases stone risk?
investigations__URINE__Metabolic & Speci.explanation: Citrate chelates calcium and inhibits crystal aggregation, making it the urine's main natural stone inhibitor. Low urinary citrate (hypocitraturia) therefore raises risk and is treated with potassium citrate. The other analytes increase stone risk when elevated, not when low.
